Benjamin Francis
BEN-juh-min FRAN-sis
proper noun
Benjamin, Hebrew “son of the right hand”; Francis, from the Latin Franciscus, “Frenchman, freeman.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Benjamin Francis (1734–1799) was a Welshman of Newcastle Emlyn, converted young and called to the Particular Baptist ministry, who for over forty years pastored the church at Horsley in Gloucestershire and itinerated tirelessly through the western counties. A preacher of uncommon warmth and a poet in both English and his native Welsh, he laboured in an era when the Baptists were emerging from a season of deadness into the fresh life of evangelical zeal, and he was among those who fanned the flame. So esteemed was his gospel labour that he was thrice invited to great London pulpits, and thrice he refused, judging his little country flock a nobler charge than the applause of the city—a choice that rebukes every minister who measures his call by the size of his hearers. His hymns and elegies, many in Welsh, stirred the affections of the chapels, and his preaching bore fruit in conversions and in churches planted. Francis wrote a moving elegy on the death of George Whitefield, joining his voice to the mourning of the awakened church. His life embodies the pastoral fidelity the Scriptures commend: content in an obscure vineyard, fervent in the pulpit, prolific with the pen, and jealous only for the honour of his Master. He stands as a Welsh forefather of the missionary awakening soon to break upon the Baptists through Carey and his circle.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Welsh Particular Baptist pastor and hymnwriter (1734–1799) who declined London for a faithful country ministry.

A Welsh Particular Baptist minister born at Newcastle Emlyn.

Pastor at Horsley, Gloucestershire, for over forty years, and a tireless itinerant.

A hymnwriter and poet in both English and Welsh who stirred the chapels.

Thrice declined prominent London pulpits to keep his country flock.

A forerunner of the Baptist missionary awakening in the western counties.

📖 Key Scripture

1Co 4:2 — "Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful."

Joh 21:16 — "He saith to him again the second time, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me? He saith unto him, Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee. He saith unto him, Feed my sheep."

Act 20:24 — "But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God."

Psa 126:6 — "He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle of pastoral contentment in an obscure charge.

expand to see more

Francis is preserved because his thrice-refused London pulpit exposes an idol the age still bows to: the notion that a ministry’s worth is weighed by its platform. He judged a hidden Gloucestershire flock a richer stewardship than the applause of the metropolis, and so preached with his feet a sermon the ambitious sorely need.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is faithfulness in the appointed vineyard—that the LORD requires stewards to be found faithful, not famous. Francis’s song and his sacrifice call the church back to a ministry measured by love for Christ’s sheep rather than the size of the crowd, and to the sowing of precious seed that returns, in God’s time, with sheaves of rejoicing.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Francis’s ministry roots the pastoral office in faithful stewardship and love for the flock over worldly advancement.

expand to see more

The steward’s one requirement, that he “be found faithful” (1Co 4:2).

Christ’s charge, “Feed my sheep,” as the measure of pastoral love (Joh 21:16).

Paul’s resolve to finish his course and testify the gospel of grace (Act 20:24).

The promise to the weeping sower of a harvest of sheaves (Psa 126:6).

The Welsh chapels’ awakening as seedbed of the coming missionary zeal.
